edits.find:
• Proximity and Visibility: Disclosures must appear immediately before or alongside the recommendation, visible to readers without requiring them to scroll down or click an ambiguous "Terms" link. Placing a disclosure solely in the website footer does not comply with FTC guidelines.
  • Unambiguous Language: Use straightforward phrasing that an average consumer easily understands (such as "We may earn a commission if you purchase through our links, at no extra cost to you") rather than cryptic jargon or vague terminology.
edits.replace:
• Proximity and Visibility: The FTC says the disclosure should be as close as possible to the recommendation and hard to miss. A single disclosure on your home page is not sufficient, readers may miss one at the bottom of a page, and a disclosure hidden behind a link (such as a button labelled "Disclosure") is easy to avoid.
  • Unambiguous Language: Use plain wording such as the FTC's own example, "I get commissions for purchases made through links in this post," or a short label like "Paid link" right next to an affiliate link.
edits.reason: Aligned disclosure rules with the FTC FAQ text (verified)

edits.find: According to published Google Search Central Affiliate Guidelines, sites that participate in affiliate programs must provide substantial added value beyond the merchant's original copy. Merely aggregating product descriptions or duplicating manufacturer specs is classified as thin, low-value content.
edits.replace: Google's spam policies describe “thin affiliation”—affiliate pages that copy merchant descriptions or reviews without adding original content—as a violation, while noting that not every site in an affiliate program is thin. Original reviews, testing, comparisons, and pricing information are examples of added value.
edits.reason: Old affiliate-guidelines URL now redirects to spam policies; wording aligned with current page

edits.find: Furthermore, Google requires publishers to qualify commercial links using appropriate link relationship attributes. Every outbound affiliate hyperlink should carry either rel="sponsored" or rel="nofollow" (or both: rel="sponsored nofollow") to signal to web crawlers that the link involves a paid commercial arrangement. Failure to properly qualify monetized links can trigger manual search ranking actions for unnatural outbound links. Complying with digital publishing standards championed by organizations such as the Interactive Advertising Bureau (IAB) guarantees that your web property remains resilient across algorithmic updates.
edits.replace: Google also asks publishers to qualify paid links: mark them with rel="sponsored" (preferred) or rel="nofollow", which remains acceptable. Unqualified paid links can violate Google's link-spam policy.
edits.reason: Aligned with Google's qualify-outbound-links page; removed "guarantees" claim and IAB filler
